proposals.name: Anonymized code-repo link boilerplate presence
proposals.instruction: Read the abstract text only. On a 0-10 scale, rate how much of the text consists of an explicit code/data-availability sentence containing a repository placeholder or URL (e.g., phrases like 'code is available at', 'anonymous.4open.science', a GitHub/Zenodo/HuggingFace link, or an anonymized-link placeholder). 0 = no such sentence or link appears anywhere in the text; 10 = the text contains a fully explicit availability sentence with a visible link/placeholder string. Score only how much of this boilerplate is present in the text -- do NOT judge whether releasing code is a good practice or whether the paper's contribution is strong.
proposals.upstream_parent: author/lab's established practice of publishing anonymized code repositories (a subfield/venue reproducibility norm)
proposals.rationale: Explicit anonymous.4open.science-style links appear in 8 of 30 dense_low_card_high rows (R03, R11, R16, R31, R35, R37, R41, R43) but essentially only once (R38) among the 30 dense_high_card_low rows -- a template/checklist habit the scorecard's fixed criteria may reward mechanically, not a marker of the work's underlying quality.

proposals.name: Unfilled placeholder / filler token in text
proposals.instruction: Read the abstract text only. On a 0-10 scale, rate how much the text contains an obviously unfilled template placeholder or generic filler standing in for a specific value that a finished document would normally contain (e.g., a literal bracket-style placeholder token, the bare word 'anonymized' used as a noun in place of a real link or name, 'TBD', or similar unedited filler). 0 = no such filler token anywhere; 10 = the text is dominated by unfilled placeholder text. Score only the presence/extent of unfilled filler tokens -- do NOT judge whether leaving such a placeholder reflects poorly on the work.
proposals.upstream_parent: rushed, last-minute production of the submission text under deadline pressure, leaving template placeholders unedited
proposals.rationale: R39 literally reads 'The code is available at: $<$placeholder$>$.' and R34 reads 'Our code is available at anonymized.' -- both are raw, unedited template tokens rather than content, a production-process artifact unrelated to the described method's quality.

proposals.name: Unrendered LaTeX/markdown source syntax leakage
proposals.instruction: Read the abstract text only. On a 0-10 scale, rate how much of the text contains raw, unrendered markup syntax from a source format -- for example LaTeX commands and delimiters (\emph{...}, \textit{...}, \url{...}, bare dollar-sign math like $75\%$ or $N$), or unrendered markdown link syntax like '[label](url)'. 0 = the text reads as clean plain prose with no visible markup syntax; 10 = markup syntax is pervasive throughout the text. Score only how much raw markup is visible -- do NOT judge whether this makes the writing worse or better.
proposals.upstream_parent: production pipeline artifact: the abstract text was extracted or copy-pasted from LaTeX/markdown source without a cleanup or rendering pass before being placed in this corpus
proposals.rationale: R05 shows raw LaTeX like '\emph{public data samples}' and '$75\%$ accuracy... $\varepsilon=2,\delta=10^{-5}$', and R37 shows '\textsf{S}em\textsf{A}ntic' and '\url{...}' -- these are copy-paste artifacts of the originating document format, not properties of the underlying research.

proposals.name: Inline (Author, Year) citation embedded in abstract
proposals.instruction: Read the abstract text only. On a 0-10 scale, rate how much the text contains an explicit parenthetical citation to a specific named prior work in author-year form (e.g., '(Smith et al., 2023)') embedded directly in the abstract's sentences. 0 = no such inline citation appears; 10 = the abstract is structured around multiple such inline citations. Score only whether/how much this citation form is present -- do NOT judge whether citing that particular prior work is appropriate or whether the citation reflects strong scholarship.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's depth of embedding in a narrow, specific sub-literature -- a practice more common among researchers who work closely and continuously in one recent line of related work
proposals.rationale: R33 names '(Reddi et al., 2023)' and R50 names '(Anil et al., 2021)' directly inside the abstract prose, a citation habit most abstracts in this slice do not use at all, which may track who wrote the abstract and how they habitually position their work rather than the work's quality.

proposals.name: Density of generic academic transition/hedge connectives
proposals.instruction: Read the abstract text only. On a 0-10 scale, rate how densely the text uses generic academic transition and hedge phrases such as 'Moreover,', 'Furthermore,', 'Additionally,', 'To this end,', 'To address this,', 'Notably,', or 'However,' as sentence openers. 0 = none of these connective phrases appear; 10 = nearly every sentence opens with one of these stock connectives. Score only the density of this scaffolding language -- do NOT judge whether the writing is well-organized or persuasive.
proposals.upstream_parent: heavy multi-pass editing or writing assistance in composing the abstract (co-author revision rounds or AI-assisted polishing), which tends to smooth prose into standard connective scaffolding
proposals.rationale: R41 strings together 'However,... Moreover, we introduce...' and R43 uses 'Additionally,... To address these issues,...' -- a dense scaffold of stock transitions that reflects how heavily the prose was revised/polished, not what the underlying method achieves.

proposals.name: Density of currently-trending AI buzzwords
proposals.instruction: Read the abstract text only. On a 0-10 scale, rate how densely the text uses currently-fashionable AI terminology such as 'large language model(s)/LLM(s)', 'agent(s)', 'multimodal', 'alignment', 'safety', 'diffusion model', or 'foundation model', relative to the abstract's length. 0 = none of these terms appear; 10 = these terms saturate the text. Score only the density of this specific vocabulary -- do NOT judge whether the topic itself is important or whether the paper handles it well.
proposals.upstream_parent: social/audience effects -- reviewers and readers may pay disproportionate attention to submissions using currently-hyped vocabulary regardless of execution quality
proposals.rationale: R02 is saturated with 'large language models (LLMs)', 'value alignment', and 'jailbreak attacks', and R38 repeats 'Multimodal large language models (LLMs)' and 'multimodal capabilities' throughout -- both read as topically fashionable independent of which model favors them, since R02 is dense_low_card_high and R38 is dense_high_card_low.

proposals.name: Framed as refinement of one specific recent named predecessor
proposals.instruction: Read the abstract text only. On a 0-10 scale, rate how much the text is structured around explicitly naming and improving upon ONE specific, recently-published predecessor method or system (e.g., 'we extend the ... method', 'unlike [named prior system], we propose...'), rather than presenting the contribution as a direct, self-contained treatment of the underlying problem. 0 = the text presents a self-contained treatment of the problem with no single named predecessor being extended/critiqued; 10 = the text is centrally organized around naming and improving one specific recent predecessor. Score only how much this refinement-of-a-named-predecessor structure is present -- do NOT judge whether the resulting improvement is significant or well-executed.
proposals.upstream_parent: position in the entry stream -- how crowded/mined this specific sub-topic already was by the time this item was produced; items arriving later in an already-picked-over niche differentiate themselves by naming and refining one immediate predecessor, while items arriving earlier can present a direct/foundational solution
proposals.rationale: R18 explicitly says it is 'extending the effective hybrid latent refinement (HLR) method, which is designed for in-domain inference' and diagnoses its cross-domain failure mode, and R33 explicitly contrasts itself with 'gradual stacking (Reddi et al., 2023)' as the specific prior stage it improves on -- both read as later entries responding to one specific, already-established prior move rather than opening the topic.

proposals.name: Explicit (1)/(2)/(3)-style enumeration of components
proposals.instruction: Read the abstract text only. On a 0-10 scale, rate how much the text uses explicit numbered enumeration markers such as '(1)', '(2)', '(3)' to itemize contributions, components, or findings. 0 = no such numbered markers appear; 10 = the abstract's structure is built almost entirely around such numbered lists. Score only the presence/extent of this enumeration formatting -- do NOT judge whether the enumerated items themselves are good or well-chosen.
proposals.rationale: R14 itemizes findings as '(1) can be used to reconstruct... (2) reconstruct the original total score... (3) have a single underlying common factor', and R19 itemizes its framework as '(1) categorical learning signals... (2) perceptual learning signals' -- a template-level organizational habit rather than a property of the science.

proposals.name: Overall abstract length / elaboration verbosity
proposals.instruction: Read the abstract text only. On a 0-10 scale, rate how long and multi-paragraph-elaborated the text is (counting sentences, sub-claims, and paragraph breaks), independent of what those sentences say. 0 = a single short, terse paragraph; 10 = an unusually long, multi-paragraph abstract with many elaborated sub-points. Score only length/verbosity -- do NOT judge whether the extra length is used well or whether the content justifies it.
proposals.rationale: R17 (CerebroVoice) and R53 (SSPINNpose) run to three and two long, densely elaborated paragraphs respectively with multiple named sub-tasks and results, while R26 (SVIN) and R45 (evolutionary architecture search) are single terse paragraphs -- a length/verbosity axis that can move independently of the underlying contribution's quality.

proposals.name: Density of high-precision numeric result callouts
proposals.instruction: Read the abstract text only. On a 0-10 scale, rate how densely the text is packed with specific, high-decimal-precision numeric performance figures presented as headline results (e.g., '35.44 BLEU', '67.39% AUC-ROC', '1.24% RMSE'), as opposed to describing results only qualitatively. 0 = no precise numeric result figures appear; 10 = the text is dominated by a string of such precise numeric callouts. Score only the density of this numeric-scoreboard presentation style -- do NOT judge whether the reported numbers represent a genuinely strong result.
proposals.rationale: R07 strings together 'a new record...35.44 BLEU score...31.03 BLEU score...over 2.6 BLEU improvement...new record of 49.61 BLEU score' and R21 reports 'an AUC-ROC of 67.39% on Pythia-12B, compared to 58.90% by the second-best attack' -- both present findings as a dense scoreboard of precise decimals, a presentation-style choice separable from whether the underlying result is actually strong.

proposals.name: Headline numeric result density in the abstract
proposals.instruction: Count how much of the abstract is devoted to concrete quantitative result statements: specific benchmark numbers, percentages, deltas, speedup factors, error rates, scores, or order-of-magnitude claims attached to named datasets. Score 0 if the abstract contains no numeric performance figures at all, 5 if it contains one or two, 10 if numeric figures are pervasive and clustered into a results run. Judge only HOW MUCH numeric reporting is present. Do NOT judge whether the numbers are impressive, correct, meaningful, or well-chosen, and do not reward or penalize the abstract for having them.
proposals.rationale: Numeric saturation is a scorecard-legible surface: a criterion bank asking 'are results quantified?' fires mechanically on it. R15 stacks three BLEU records (35.44, 31.03, 49.61) and R31 leads with 67.39% vs 58.90% AUC-ROC; R37 quotes MAE 1.897e-3 vs 27.074e-3. Meanwhile R17, R43, R56 and R60 report essentially no numbers and are all dense-high/card-low. The count of digits is a writing habit, not evidence quality — an abstract can enumerate numbers from a weak benchmark or omit them while reporting a strong one.

proposals.name: Checklist-shaped rhetorical scaffolding (problem-gap-we-propose-results)
proposals.instruction: Rate how closely the abstract follows the canonical four-move template — (1) topic is important, (2) however/existing work is limited, (3) to address this we propose NAMED-METHOD, (4) experiments show it outperforms — with explicit discourse connectives ('However', 'To address this issue', 'To this end', 'Specifically', 'Extensive experiments demonstrate'). Score 0 for an abstract with no recognizable template and no such connectives, 10 for one that hits all four moves in order with multiple explicit connective phrases. Score only the EXTENT of template conformity. Do NOT judge whether following the template is good writing or whether the content behind each move is sound.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's practice in the format / venue-style socialization and editing assistance
proposals.rationale: Template conformity is exactly what a fixed criterion bank is built to detect — every slot a criterion asks about has a marked-off sentence. R24 ('However, existing... To enrich... Specifically... Moreover, we introduce... Experimental results demonstrate'), R50, R51 and R46 are near-perfect template instances and all sit card-high/dense-low. R17, R35, R56 and R60 break the template (R17 is 'three simple ideas', R56 opens with a framing metaphor) and are dense-high/card-low. Template fluency tracks how many papers the author has written in this format, not whether this paper is good.

proposals.name: Anonymous artifact link and release-promise boilerplate
proposals.instruction: Rate how prominently the abstract contains artifact-availability signalling: an anonymized code/data URL (anonymous.4open.science, an anonymized repo, a dataset host), or a promise such as 'code will be released/open-sourced upon acceptance/publication'. Score 0 for no mention of code or data availability, 5 for a bare promise with no link, 10 for an explicit live anonymized URL given prominence in the closing sentence. Score only the EXTENT of availability signalling present in the text. Do NOT judge whether releasing artifacts is good practice or whether the promise is credible.
proposals.upstream_parent: submission timing and submission-portal practice (having a polished anonymized release ready at deadline)
proposals.rationale: An availability line is a one-token match for a 'reproducibility' criterion and is cheap to add, so it inflates a scorecard without touching content quality. R37, R39, R46, R58 and R34 all carry anonymous.4open.science URLs and all are dense-low/card-high; R10, R50 and R52 carry the weaker 'upon acceptance' promise and are also card-high. Almost no dense-high/card-low row (R17, R18, R29, R35, R43, R56) mentions artifacts at all. The upstream cause is deadline logistics and lab tooling, not paper merit.

proposals.name: Branded acronym coinage with typographic staging
proposals.instruction: Rate how much of the abstract is organized around a coined product-style name for the contribution — an all-caps or CamelCase acronym, especially one introduced with a parenthetical gloss, repeated three or more times, or set off with markup (bold, \textsf, letter-highlighting that spells the acronym). Score 0 if the contribution is described without any coined name, 5 for a name introduced once and used plainly, 10 for a heavily staged acronym repeated throughout with typographic emphasis. Score only the EXTENT of naming and staging. Do NOT judge whether the name is apt, memorable, or whether naming a method is good practice.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's practice in the format / lab branding conventions
proposals.rationale: Naming is a marketing habit correlated with lab seniority and prior submissions; a criterion asking 'is the contribution clearly identified?' cannot distinguish a name from a contribution. R39 spells SAFARI out letter-by-letter in \textsf markup, R32 bolds **C**LIP/DIN**O**/**COMM**, R6 glosses LIME as 'Less Is More for MLLM Evaluation', R58 stages FHBI, R34 stages CoPS — R39, R6, R58 and R34 are all dense-low/card-high. R18, R35, R43 and R56 name nothing and are dense-high/card-low. The presence of a brand is orthogonal to whether the method works.

proposals.name: Layperson-legible motivating opener versus in-the-weeds cold open
proposals.instruction: Rate how much of the opening third of the abstract is spent on broadly accessible motivation — an everyday example, a societal or scientific stake, a human-intuition anchor — before any technical machinery appears. Score 0 for an abstract that opens directly on technical objects assuming full subfield fluency, 10 for one whose opening is entirely non-technical scene-setting understandable to any reader. Score only WHERE ON THIS SPECTRUM the opening falls. Do NOT judge whether accessible or technical openings are better, and do not treat either end as a merit signal.
proposals.rationale: A dense reader rewards vivid, coherent framing that a slot-filling bank cannot score; conversely a bank rewards the technically dense cold open as 'precise'. R1 opens with toy ducks and real ducks at the park and R56 with an observer traveling around a space — both dense-high/card-low with card_pct at .065 and .202. R28 (bootstrap rate definitions), R11 and R45 open cold on technical apparatus and are card-high/dense-low. Accessibility of the first sentence is a stylistic register choice, not a property of the underlying work.

proposals.name: Deference density: hedges, citations to prior frameworks, incremental positioning
proposals.instruction: Rate how much the abstract positions itself as an extension, refinement, or correction of a specific named prior method or framework rather than as a standalone proposal — count named-predecessor mentions ('extending the HLR method', 'builds upon prover-verifier games (Anil et al., 2021)', 'compared with the original AdvGAN', 'contrary to previous findings'), plus hedging qualifiers ('preliminary', 'early results', 'suggests', 'to a limited extent'). Score 0 for an abstract that names no predecessor and hedges nothing, 10 for one saturated with named predecessors and hedges. Score only the EXTENT of deferential/incremental framing. Do NOT judge whether incrementality or hedging is a virtue or a defect.
proposals.upstream_parent: author seniority and position in the field's citation network; reviewer-response conditioning from prior submission rounds
proposals.rationale: Explicit predecessor anchoring gives a scorecard easy 'positioned in related work' points while hedges cost a dense reader confidence — or the reverse, depending on which model. R5 leans on extending HLR, R46 on extending AdvGAN, R28 on contradicting previous findings; all three are dense-low/card-high. R21 hedges hard ('present early training results') and R41 hedges ('preliminary computational experiments') and both are dense-high/card-low, so the hedge is not what the scorecard sees. The upstream factor — how embedded the author is in a lineage — is not the same as how good the paper is.

proposals.name: Benchmark/dataset name-dropping density
proposals.instruction: Count how many named, recognizable benchmarks, datasets, or model families the abstract lists by proper name (e.g., ImageNet, CIFAR-10, SuperGLUE, MMLU, WikiTableQuestions, Pythia, GPT-4o, ShapeNet, LibriSpeech, VTAB-1K). Score 0 for none named, 3 for one or two, 7 for three to five, 10 for six or more or an explicitly enumerated list. Score only the COUNT AND PROMINENCE of named resources. Do NOT judge whether the chosen benchmarks are appropriate, standard, hard, or sufficient for the claim.
proposals.upstream_parent: compute and engineering resources available to the producing lab
proposals.rationale: Roster length is a proxy for lab compute budget, which is upstream of both the text and (separately) of perceived thoroughness; a bank criterion for 'evaluation breadth' reads it directly. R3 lists WebQuestions/TriviaQA/SearchQA/Quasar-T/FIGER and R8 lists seven models plus four languages; R31 names Pythia, GPT-Neo, Wikipedia, MIMIR and R58 names VTAB-1K's 19 datasets. R31, R58, R37 and R42 are all dense-low/card-high, while R29 (one 95k-parameter network), R44 and R60 name almost nothing and are dense-high/card-low. Counting nouns is not assessing evidence.

proposals.name: First-obvious-reading versus late-riff-on-a-crowded-topic register
proposals.instruction: Rate how much the abstract reads as a late entry into an already-crowded line of work rather than a first, obvious pass at its problem. Late-entry fingerprints: presupposing a named subfield or acronym as already established ('TTA-IC approaches', 'existing MIAs', 'reflection-driven reasoning', 'AdvGAN'), correcting or narrowing a specific existing fix, targeting a residual gap the text itself calls 'barely explored' or 'underexplored' WITHIN an established line, or numbering itself against a wave of prior variants. First-pass fingerprints: introducing the problem itself, claiming a 'first' task or dataset, or defining terms from scratch. Score 0 for a pure first-pass reading, 10 for a deep late-entry riff. Score only WHERE the abstract sits on this arrival-order spectrum. Do NOT judge whether early or late entry is better work.
proposals.upstream_parent: position in the entry stream — where this submission falls in the arrival order of a topic wave, and how crowded that topic's queue already is
proposals.rationale: MODE 3. Arrival order is invisible but leaves a strong trace: late entrants must presuppose vocabulary and target residual gaps, which reads to a criterion bank as 'well-situated and specific' and to a dense reader as narrow. R5 presupposes TTA-IC and HLR and refines a known method; R31 presupposes MIAs; R34 presupposes reflection-driven and experience-assisted reasoning; R51 presupposes the SL/TD stitching debate — R5 is the one dense-high exception while R31, R34 and R51 are all card-high/dense-low. Against them R43 (introducing neural interactive proofs), R56 (a framing from scratch) and R1 (setting up the problem itself) read as first passes and are dense-high/card-low. Position in a wave is not paper quality; both good and bad papers arrive late.

proposals.name: Non-anglophone-editing fingerprints and register slips
proposals.instruction: Rate the density of textual traces of heavy or uneven editing passes: Latinate formal-register substitutions used where a plain word would serve ('Nonetheless', 'commendable', 'endeavors to', 'in an endeavor to', 'the prevailing', 'adeptly', 'crucially relies'), article or preposition irregularities, unusual collocations, promotional adjectives applied to one's own work ('remarkable', 'innovative', 'superior', 'great advantages'), and inconsistent typography within one abstract (mixed straight/curly quotes, hard-wrapped lines, mixed LaTeX and Unicode math, stray markup). Score 0 for uniformly idiomatic, typographically consistent prose, 10 for pervasive traces. Score only the EXTENT of these traces. Do NOT judge whether the prose is good, and explicitly do NOT penalize or reward non-native English — you are counting fingerprints, not rating writing.
proposals.upstream_parent: who produced the text and their editing/assistance resources (professional copy-editing, senior-coauthor rewriting, LLM polishing)
proposals.rationale: Access to editing is upstream of the text and correlates with lab resources rather than with result quality, and the two models read it oppositely: a dense reader is sensitive to register, a rubric bank is not. R10 ('In an endeavor to enhance the efficacy', 'the prevailing proof accuracy', 'intricate issues that persist'), R51 ('commendable results', 'endeavors to'), R54 ('adeptly reverse-aligned', 'acts as a whistleblower') and R50 ('great potential') are all dense-low/card-high. R40 is hard-wrapped mid-word ('chal-lenging'), R6 mixes a Unicode right-quote into 'MLLMs' captioning'. R17, R18 and R35 are plain and idiomatic and are dense-high/card-low. Editing budget is not scientific merit.

proposals.name: Resource-contribution framing (benchmark/dataset/suite as the deliverable)
proposals.instruction: Rate how much the abstract presents its primary contribution as a shipped RESOURCE — a benchmark, dataset, environment suite, simulator, or evaluation harness — as opposed to a method, algorithm, analysis, or theoretical result. Fingerprints: counts of items/tasks/splits ('900 dev and 1800 test problems', '4 modalities and 20 organs', a named environment list), 'we curate/collect/establish benchmarks', 'publicly available on Zenodo and GitHub', 'first publicly accessible'. Score 0 for a pure method or theory paper with no resource deliverable, 10 for an abstract whose whole spine is the resource and its inventory. Score only the EXTENT of resource framing. Do NOT judge whether resource papers are valuable or whether this resource is well built.
proposals.upstream_parent: producing group's data-access and annotation-labor capacity (clinical/institutional partnerships, annotator budget), plus the venue's shifting appetite for dataset tracks
proposals.rationale: Resource abstracts mechanically satisfy many bank criteria at once — scope, coverage, availability, evaluation breadth — because inventories are countable, while a dense reader may find no idea in them. R47 (CerebroVoice sEEG dataset, Zenodo/GitHub), R53 (Face-Human-Bench, 900/1800 problems, 25 MLLMs), R59 (HIVEX five-environment suite), R55 (GenNet simulator), R20 (4 modalities, 20 organs) and R6 (LIME) are all dense-low/card-high, several extremely so (R47 card .917, R6 card .725 at dense .019). No dense-high/card-low row is resource-shaped. Whether a group could assemble a dataset reflects institutional access and annotation money, which is upstream of the text and distinct from quality.

proposals.name: Abstract length
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, how much unusually long, multi-paragraph, or verbally expansive prose is present? Judge only extent, not whether the feature is good or evidence of quality.
proposals.rationale: Length can alter attention and representation while carrying no intrinsic evidence of merit. R01 and R17 contain especially extended multi-stage descriptions.

proposals.name: Markup residue
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, how much LaTeX, boldface, footnote, URL, line-break, or other formatting residue is visible? Judge only extent, not whether the feature is good or evidence of quality.
proposals.rationale: Formatting artifacts can trigger stylistic associations without describing technical substance. R05 includes a footnote, while R25 and R37 visibly retain specialized markup.

proposals.name: Acronym branding
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, how much acronym-heavy naming, coined terminology, or branded method language is present? Judge only extent, not whether the feature is good or evidence of quality.
proposals.rationale: Authors practiced in conference conventions may package ideas with memorable names, which can affect textual salience independently of merit; that practice may also accompany genuine expertise. R02 uses SSPINNpose, while R24 and R51 use several branded components.

proposals.name: Benchmark arithmetic
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, how much the abstract foregrounds exact percentages, metric values, margins, speedups, counts, or leaderboard-style comparisons? Judge only extent, not whether the feature is good or evidence of quality.
proposals.rationale: Competitive evaluation culture can encourage conspicuous numerical claims that attract attention without establishing broad merit, while also motivating more careful experimentation. R02 and R45 foreground many exact figures, and R58 emphasizes a large percentage improvement.

proposals.name: Formalism density
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, how much dense mathematical notation, theorem terminology, asymptotic language, or formal optimization vocabulary is present? Judge only extent, not whether the feature is good or evidence of quality.
proposals.rationale: Disciplinary style can make text appear technically authoritative without the notation itself proving substance; formal training may also support genuinely rigorous work. R04 uses regret notation, R37 discusses Weyl's Theorem, and R39 uses extensive norm and optimization terminology.

proposals.name: Artifact signaling
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, how much the abstract mentions code, data, demos, repositories, open sourcing, or public availability? Judge only extent, not whether the feature is good or evidence of quality.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's familiarity with submission and artifact conventions
proposals.rationale: Artifact language can function as a reproducibility signal even when the text gives no evidence about the artifacts themselves; artifact-oriented practice can also support real reproducibility. R01 mentions code and data, while R13 and R51 mention released resources.

proposals.name: Fashion-topic vocabulary
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, how much vocabulary associated with currently fashionable themes such as LLMs, multimodality, agents, alignment, or foundation models is present? Judge only extent, not whether the feature is good or evidence of quality.
proposals.rationale: Topic fashion can change textual familiarity and salience without changing the underlying contribution. R03 and R26 use extensive multimodal-LLM terminology, while R53 centers alignment and jailbreak language.

proposals.name: Copyedited fluency
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, how much standardized copyedited fluency is visible through consistent grammar, parallel syntax, smooth transitions, and uniform professional phrasing? Judge only extent, not whether the feature is good or evidence of quality.
proposals.rationale: Editing or assistance can produce a polished surface that is mistaken for substance, while clearer editing may also improve genuine communication. R06 and R40 use highly uniform polished exposition, and R54 maintains consistently formal prose across a broad motivation.

proposals.name: Deadline-compression residue
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, how much uneven detail, abrupt compression, dangling explanation, local grammatical error, or placeholder text suggest hurried assembly? Judge only extent, not whether the feature is good or evidence of quality.
proposals.rationale: Deadline pressure can leave visible assembly residue that affects textual processing independently of the underlying work, and it can also affect the work itself. R49 contains a conspicuous placeholder, while R38 has local grammatical irregularities and R01 compresses several technical transitions unevenly.

proposals.name: Late-riff framing
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, how much the abstract assumes a settled conversation and presents a narrow contrastive refinement rather than introducing the problem from scratch? Judge only extent, not whether the feature is good or evidence of quality.
proposals.rationale: A late-arriving entry in a crowded container might leave a textual fingerprint of compressed background, repeated field framing, and a narrowly differentiated hook; the fingerprint is not actual position or merit. R28 and R43 use dense contrastive positioning, while R58 assumes extensive prior prompt-optimization context.

proposals.name: Promotional superlative load
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 for the extent of promotional adjectives, adverbs, and emphatic claims in the text; judge only their presence, not whether they are justified or good.
proposals.rationale: Such language can trigger stylistic reactions without measuring contribution quality. It appears in R01, R12, R54, and R57.

proposals.name: Acronym and method-brand density
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 for the extent of newly introduced acronyms, stylized names, and branded method labels; do not judge whether the names are useful or the methods are good.
proposals.rationale: Memorable naming can affect textual salience independently of substance. Examples include HIVEX in R01, COMM in R12, and SAFARI in R16.

proposals.name: Numerical result saturation
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 for the density of precise numerical results, percentages, ratios, dataset counts, speedups, or benchmark deltas; do not judge whether the numbers indicate quality.
proposals.rationale: Specific figures provide attention-grabbing concreteness, while reporting practice may also reflect genuine experimental strength. This fingerprint appears in R02, R07, R17, and R40.

proposals.name: Release-and-link signaling
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 for the extent of code, data, demo, repository, hosting-site, or future-release references; do not judge whether the release is complete or valuable.
proposals.rationale: Availability signals can influence textual impressions, while release practice may also accompany genuine reproducibility. Examples occur in R11, R13, R53, and R58.

proposals.name: Production-format artifacts
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 for visible formatting or production artifacts such as raw markup, escaped commands, broken hyphenation, placeholders, footnotes, or inconsistent spacing; do not judge whether the formatting is good or bad.
proposals.rationale: Submission or conversion artifacts can create nuisance variation unrelated to the research. They are visible in R10, R16, R31, and R33.

proposals.name: Abstract-template sequencing
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 for the extent to which the abstract follows a formulaic problem-gap-method-results-impact sequence with stock transitions; do not judge whether the sequence communicates well.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's practice in the abstract format
proposals.rationale: Familiar structure can make a text easier to process, while practiced abstract writing may also reflect genuine communication skill. The pattern is evident in R03, R14, R40, and R44.

proposals.name: Community lineage shorthand
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 for unexplained insider shorthand, canonical benchmark names, inherited model references, and field-specific lineage cues; do not judge whether the terminology is technically appropriate.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's community embeddedness and field familiarity
proposals.rationale: Community-recognizable cues can facilitate rapid interpretation, while field familiarity may also support genuine technical work. Examples include R19, R36, R50, and R55.

proposals.name: Trend-and-stakes framing
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 for fashionable umbrella framing and broad-impact language involving agents, foundation models, real-world impact, safety, scientific discovery, or multimodal systems; do not judge whether the stated importance is deserved.
proposals.rationale: Current-topic framing can attract attention independently of contribution quality. Comparable framing appears in R01, R18, R35, and R57.

proposals.name: Priority-claim language
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 for explicit priority or originality claims such as first, novel, new record, unprecedented, or to our knowledge; do not judge whether the claim is true or important.
proposals.rationale: Priority language can alter salience without establishing substantive quality. It occurs in R03, R13, R16, R34, and R43.

proposals.name: Early-entry framing
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 for an early-entry textual fingerprint: broad textbook motivation, canonical problem setup, extensive context, and little assumed background; do not judge whether this framing is clear or valuable.
proposals.rationale: An item written as an initial, obvious framing may differ stylistically from a later riff that assumes familiar context, despite equal substance. Early-entry cues are visible in R01, R20, R35, and R53.

proposals.name: Named-system branding prominence
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the extent to which the abstract uses a proper-noun system or dataset name (e.g., a coined acronym) as the central organising device of the text -- repeating it, using it as the subject of sentences, and presenting its unveiling as the primary contribution. Do not judge whether the name is catchy or the system is good; score only how much naming dominates the structure.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's branding/marketing practice in the format
proposals.rationale: A practice of foregrounding coined names may correlate with polished, product-oriented work but is not itself quality. R02 leads with 'CerebroVoice' and 'MoBSE' as headline contributions; R47 repeatedly foregrounds 'NIERT'; R56 stages 'SAFARI' with stylised typography. By contrast R07, R25, and R35 present ideas with little or no branding.

proposals.name: Code and data availability disclosure
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the extent to which the abstract contains explicit statements about code, data, or repository availability -- including URLs, phrases like 'publicly available', 'open-sourced upon acceptance/publication', or named hosting platforms (Zenodo, GitHub, HuggingFace). Score the presence of these disclosures regardless of whether the code actually exists; do not judge whether releasing code is good.
proposals.upstream_parent: submission strategy / community norms around open science
proposals.rationale: Mentioning code release in an abstract is a community-norm signal, not a quality signal; it may reflect submission-strategy coaching or venue expectations. R02, R14, R22, R32, R40, R45, R47, and R56 all include explicit availability disclosures, while R07, R10, R25, and R35 contain none.

proposals.name: LaTeX source-formatting artifact density
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the density of LaTeX-specific formatting commands visible in the abstract text, including \textit, \textsf, \emph, \url, \footnote, escaped characters (\%, \$), inline math mode delimiters ($...$), and \times. Count artifacts per sentence; do not judge whether the formatting looks professional.
proposals.rationale: Raw LaTeX artifacts in a plain-text abstract reflect copy-paste provenance and editing pipeline, not content quality. R21 is saturated with $32\times$, $3\times$, $9-16\%$; R14 carries \footnote and $5\times$; R56 uses \textsf and \url. Clean-prose abstracts like R07, R10, and R35 show almost none.

proposals.name: Multi-paragraph visual segmentation
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the extent to which the abstract is broken into visually distinct paragraphs separated by blank lines, as opposed to a single continuous block of text. Higher scores mean more paragraph breaks. Do not judge whether paragraphing improves readability.
proposals.rationale: Whether an abstract arrives as one block or several reflects formatting conventions of the source venue or template, not the underlying work. R02, R03, R05, and R53 are split into multiple paragraphs; R07, R10, R35, and R55 are single flowing blocks despite comparable content density.

proposals.name: Specific quantitative result reporting
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the density of specific numerical performance figures reported in the abstract (accuracy percentages, BLEU scores, speedup factors, error rates, etc.). Count distinct numerical claims; do not judge whether the numbers are impressive or the evaluation is rigorous.
proposals.rationale: An emphasis on packing specific metrics into the abstract reflects a results-forward reporting culture that may correlate with thoroughness but is not itself quality. R16 reports three BLEU scores; R33 cites AUC-ROC of 67.39%; R50 gives 75% accuracy vs. 68%. Abstracts like R07, R25, and R55 report qualitative or comparative findings without a cluster of specific numbers.

proposals.name: Currently-trendy terminology saturation
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the density of currently fashionable ML/AI buzzwords and phrases in the abstract -- terms such as 'large language model(s)/LLM', 'GPT', 'multimodal', 'foundation model', 'alignment', 'in-context learning', 'diffusion', 'zero-shot/few-shot', 'agent(s)'. Count occurrences; do not judge whether the topic is important.
proposals.rationale: Writing in the vocabulary of a current research wave may correlate with relevance but is not quality; it reflects the author's position in a trend cycle. R48 deploys 'LLMs', 'jailbreak', 'value alignment', 'open-source'; R60 stacks 'multimodal', 'tool use', 'agents'; R15 uses 'LLMs', 'unlearning', 'alignment'. Abstracts on less trendy topics (R24, R55, R58) score low on this surface.

proposals.name: Enumerative template-connective density
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the frequency of formulaic structural connectives that segment the abstract into enumerated sub-points: 'Specifically', 'Firstly', 'Secondly', 'In detail', 'Notably', 'Furthermore', 'To this end', 'Moreover'. Count occurrences; do not judge whether the connectives aid clarity.
proposals.rationale: Heavy use of template connectives signals a formulaic writing pipeline rather than content depth. R02 chains 'Specifically'; R14 stacks 'Firstly' and 'Secondly'; R41 opens a detail block with 'Specifically'. Abstracts that integrate transitions more naturally (R07, R10, R35) score lower.

proposals.name: Applied-domain foregrounding
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the extent to which the abstract foregrounds a specific real-world application domain (e.g., healthcare, autonomous driving, ecology, mobile networks, brain-computer interfaces, planetary exploration) as a primary motivating context, as opposed to presenting general-purpose ML methodology. Do not judge whether the application is important.
proposals.upstream_parent: applied research community affiliation and norms
proposals.rationale: Application-domain framing may correlate with practical impact but is not a quality dimension of the ML contribution itself; it reflects the authors' community and funding context. R02 foregrounds invasive brain sensing; R34 leads with medical image sequences; R53 frames around autonomous driving. General-method abstracts like R07, R24, and R55 avoid domain-specific framing entirely.

proposals.name: Genre-crowding saturation signal
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the extent to which the abstract reads as one entry in an already-saturated submission genre -- signalling this by referencing many existing approaches, framing itself as a refinement among numerous prior works, and using recognisable boilerplate from a crowded topic area. A low score means the abstract reads as occupying a less crowded niche. Do not judge whether the topic is overstudied or worthwhile.
proposals.upstream_parent: position in the entry stream / genre saturation
proposals.rationale: Where a submission falls in the topical crowd of a contest pool is a positional artefact, not quality. R20 ('Face-Human-Bench'), R45 ('Less Is More for MLLM Evaluation'), and R48 (LLM jailbreak/alignment) each read as entries in heavily populated genres with many close neighbours. R07 (traveling-observer framework), R24 (decision diagrams for norm-bounding), and R55 (preference-based RMAB) read as occupying thinner niches.

proposals.name: External named-system reference density
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the number of distinct external named models, systems, datasets, or benchmarks referenced by proper name in the abstract (e.g., BERT, GPT-4, CLIP, DINO, ImageNet, MMLU, PaLM). Count unique references; do not judge whether citing them is appropriate.
proposals.rationale: Naming many external systems may signal thorough grounding in a subfield, but density of name-drops is not quality; it reflects how embedded the authors are in a specific research network. R33 references 'Pythia and GPT-Neo'; R37 lists six benchmark suites by name; R54 enumerates seven named models. Abstracts like R07, R24, and R55 name few or no external systems.
